words.note: Common Mexican term for sweet pastries in general. French keeps the Mexican name; it corresponds roughly to 'pains sucrés / viennoiseries mexicaines'.

Can also mean cake, depending on the country. Gender differs: Spanish 'el pastel' is masculine, French 'la pâtisserie' is feminine. 'Une pâtisserie' is one pastry; 'la pâtisserie' can also mean the pastry shop. For cake, French says 'le gâteau'.
Common in Mexico. French keeps the Mexican name; in French it can be described as 'petit pain blanc croustillant'.
Keep the Mexican name 'concha' in French; it is feminine, as in Spanish. In French it can be described as 'petite brioche ronde à croûte sucrée en forme de coquillage'.
Feminine in both languages. In French it can be described as 'une sorte de chausson'. Savory ('salée') in this lesson's Reader.
Spanish 'el relleno' is masculine; French 'la garniture' is feminine. The adjective 'filled' is 'fourré' or 'garni'.
'Confiture' is the everyday French word for jam. French 'marmelade' is a false friend: it usually means a marmalade or a fruit purée.

words.english: Which one is the most typical?

words.note: Masculine default. For a concha, use 'Est-elle fourrée ?'. Spanish 'relleno' agrees with the noun, and so does the French participle. In everyday speech, 'C'est fourré ?' is also common and avoids gender.
In everyday speech, 'C'est sucré ou salé ?' is also common.
Polite form with usted. Use French 'vous' for the polite form.

words.english: Which one came out of the oven today?
words.french: Lequel est sorti du four aujourd'hui ?

reader.english: A traveler walks into a bakery in the morning.
reader.spanish: Un viajero entra a una panadería en la mañana.
reader.french: Un voyageur entre dans une boulangerie le matin.

reader.english: There are many breads and pastries on the counter.
reader.spanish: Hay muchos panes y pasteles en el mostrador.
reader.french: Il y a beaucoup de pains et de pâtisseries sur le comptoir.

reader.english: He asks: What is fresh today?
reader.french: Il demande : « Qu'est-ce qui est frais aujourd'hui ? »

reader.english: The employee says the sweet bread is from this morning.
reader.spanish: La empleada dice que el pan dulce es de esta mañana.
reader.french: L'employée dit que le pan dulce est de ce matin.

reader.english: The traveler asks: Which one is filled?
reader.french: Le voyageur demande : « Lequel est fourré ? »

reader.english: She explains that the concha is sweet and the empanada is savory.
reader.spanish: Ella explica que la concha es dulce y la empanada es salada.
reader.french: Elle explique que la concha est sucrée et que l'empanada est salée.

reader.english: He says: I want to try something typical from here.
reader.spanish: Él dice: Quiero probar algo típico de aquí.
reader.french: Il dit : « Je veux goûter quelque chose de typique d'ici. »

reader.english: The employee recommends a bolillo with cheese.
reader.spanish: La empleada recomienda un bolillo con queso.
reader.french: L'employée recommande un bolillo au fromage.

reader.english: The traveler orders a concha and a coffee, please.
reader.spanish: El viajero pide una concha y un café, por favor.
reader.french: Le voyageur commande une concha et un café, s'il vous plaît.

contextualForms.sourceEnglish: He asks what is fresh today.
contextualForms.french: Il demande ce qui est frais aujourd'hui.
contextualForms.explanationEnglish: 'Demander' is a regular -er verb, like Spanish 'preguntar', which is also regular. French uses 'demander' both to ask a question and to ask for something, where Spanish splits these into 'preguntar' and 'pedir'.

contextualForms.sourceEnglish: The employee recommends a bolillo with cheese.
contextualForms.french: L'employée recommande un bolillo au fromage.
contextualForms.explanationEnglish: Spanish 'recomendar' has an e-to-ie stem change; French 'recommander' does not. 'Au fromage' is the contraction of à + le: French uses 'au/à la' + ingredient for food descriptions where Spanish uses 'con'; 'avec du fromage' is also possible.

contextualForms.sourceEnglish: I want to try something typical from here.
contextualForms.french: Je veux goûter quelque chose de typique d'ici.
contextualForms.explanationEnglish: 'Je veux' is the irregular French form of vouloir. For food, 'goûter' is the natural equivalent of Spanish 'probar', and 'quelque chose de' + adjective is the French pattern.
'Nous goûtons' is the regular French nous form. Spanish 'probar' has an o-to-ue stem change except in the nosotros form ('probamos'); French 'goûter' is regular throughout.
Both the pronoun and the participle agree with the noun. 'Lequel est fourré ?' is masculine; for feminine items such as 'la concha' or 'l'empanada', say 'Laquelle est fourrée ?'.

Hear.promptEnglish: Listen to the French sentence from the Reader in which the traveler asks his first question, and write the whole line you hear.
Hear.targetFrench: Il demande : « Qu'est-ce qui est frais aujourd'hui ? »

Type.promptEnglish: Type the polite French question for 'What do you recommend?' (vous form).

Say.promptEnglish: Say in French the traveler's quoted words from this Reader line: 'I want to try something typical from here.'
Say.targetFrench: Je veux goûter quelque chose de typique d'ici.

Write.promptEnglish: Write the French sentence for 'The traveler orders a concha and a coffee, please.'
Write.targetFrench: Le voyageur commande une concha et un café, s'il vous plaît.

objectivesEnglish: As the traveler, ask the employee what is fresh today.
Ask whether the concha or the empanada is filled, and whether each is sweet or savory.
Say you want to try something typical from here.
Ask for a recommendation using the polite 'vous' form, and react to the employee's recommendation of a bolillo with cheese.
Order a concha and a coffee politely.
speaking.closureFrench: Voilà votre concha et votre café. Bonne journée !

qualifiedReviewQuestions.questionEnglish: For 'pastry' (Spanish 'pastel'), should the French answer be 'la pâtisserie' or 'la viennoiserie' in a Mexican panadería scene, given that 'pastel' can mean cake in some countries and 'la pâtisserie' can also mean the pastry shop?
Is 'la confiture' the right French gloss for Mexican Spanish 'mermelada' in this lesson's context, and is the false-friend note on 'marmelade' accurate for general (non-regulatory) French usage?

Should masculine 'Lequel est fourré ?' and 'Est-il fourré ?' be kept, or should gender-neutral 'C'est fourré ?' be the default, with 'Laquelle est fourrée ?' taught for the feminine concha and empanada?

Is it acceptable to keep the Spanish borrowings 'bolillo', 'concha', 'empanada' and 'pan dulce' unchanged in French, with the genders le / la / l' (feminine) / le, and to give the French descriptions only in notes?
Is 'brioche' an accurate enough French description of a concha, or should it be described as a 'petit pain sucré à croûte de sucre'?
Is 'la garniture' the best everyday word for a pastry 'filling' (relleno), or would 'la farce' (savory) or 'la crème' (sweet) fit better?
Should the narrative 's'il vous plaît' in line 9 (also the Write target) be kept for source fidelity, or put in quotes or dropped for natural French?
Should the more formal 'Est-ce sucré ou salé ?' stay as the main answer, or should spoken 'C'est sucré ou salé ?' replace it or be accepted alongside it?
